newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Envoys explain Hong Kong return to Russia.
newsitem.headline: Envoys explain Hong Kong return to Russia.

text.p: Three days from Hong Kong's handover to China and many miles away, British and Chinese diplomats waged a public relations battle on Friday, putting their spin on an event Russia may well find illuminating.

"We have waited for decades to see this event and here it comes," Chinese charge d'affaires Guan Hengguan told reporters. "The hearts of the Hong Kong masses are now with Beijing hailing the re-unification policies of the central government."

British Ambassador Sir Andrew Wood shared Guan's optimism but emphasised other angles, focusing mainly on Beijing's promise not to change things dramatically in the flourishing region for another 50 years.

"The handover is taking place on a legal basis," Wood said, speaking in Russian at a separate news conference soon afterwards. "Hong Kong retains an independent judicial system, market economy, free press and other liberties.

"I think we may be proud of the way we are parting with the empire and I think there are some parallels with Russia which carries out a similar process with dignity," he added. On July 1, Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule after 156 years as a British colony.

Russia, widely seen as the backbone of a huge Euro-Asian empire which collapsed together with the Soviet Union in 1991, is shaping new relations with former Soviet republics soured by mutual suspicions and recriminations.

The Kremlin also faces the tricky task of keeping together a mosaic of independent-minded regions and ethnic republics which form the Russian Federation. At least one of them, the southern rebel region of Chechnya, appears committed to secede.
But in drawing on the Hong Kong handover as a model for Russia, many in Moscow and beyond would rather be in Beijing's shoes than London's.

"The policy of the Chinese leaders on the territorial issue should be a model for Russian political leaders tackling the future of Sevastopol, Crimea and some other historically Russian territories," a nationalist group, the Russian Popular Union, said in a statement on Thursday.
Influential nationalists urge the Kremlin to take under its control Ukraine's Russian-speaking Crimean peninsula and its port of Sevastopol, home to the former Soviet Black Sea fleet.
They also want back Russian-populated northern parts of Kazakhstan.
President Boris Yeltsin has never backed such demands and signed a political treaty with Kiev last month which finally confirmed the inviolability of the existing border with Ukraine.

"China waited for its time and the time has come for it to take back the colony," the Union's leader Sergei Baburin has said. "But of course you have to be China, strong and attractive, to make others respect your position."
The Kremlin, which seeks stronger ties with China, is sending Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov to take part in the transition ceremonies on July 1.

"Moscow believes that this event may be an example of a civilised, unconfrontational solution of a problem which touches the interests of many states," a Foreign Ministry spokesman told a news briefing on Thursday.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin is on a visit to China and Russian news agencies quoted members of his delegation as saying President Boris Yeltsin is likely to visit Beijing later this year.

Yeltsin has made China a foreign policy priority and urged Russians to take an interest in the region. But many Russians, with problems closer to home and their wallets, are far less interested in world affairs -- including the Hong Kong handover.
